slides.0.title: Style and Tasting
slides.0.subtitle: Rancio, age and aroma stages, and a tasting framework
slides.1.title: Rancio: the hallmark of old brandy
slides.1.highlights.0.title: What rancio is
slides.1.highlights.0.content: A loose trade term for the complex aromas that appear after long oak ageing: old leather, mushrooms, soy sauce, grilled almonds, raisins and dried fruit (Difford's Guide)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Cognac stages
slides.1.highlights.1.content: It appears after roughly ten years; about 10–15 years: vanillin, floral, nutty; 16–30: curry, saffron, ginger, candied dried fruit; 30–50: old tawny port and Madeira notes, cedar, cigar box; 50+: lychee, sandalwood (Difford's Guide)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Very old spirits
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Very old Cognac is often moved into glass demijohns to avoid taking on bitter woody flavours
slides.1.content: The year bands are approximate and vary by source.
slides.2.title: Armagnac aroma stages
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Young
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Heat and cooked notes on the nose with concentrated fruity and floral notes from the distillation (armagnac.fr)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Mature
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Spirit meets wood and pastry notes appear; the shift from VSOP to Hors d'Age is gradual, not sharp (armagnac.fr)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Old
slides.2.highlights.2.content: After about twenty years many Armagnacs show rancio (armagnac.fr)
slides.2.content: Armagnac keeps more congeners, so it shows more character young than Cognac.
slides.3.title: A tasting framework
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Appearance
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Colour hints at oak contact and age, but the EU allows caramel colouring, so colour alone is not proof of age
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Nose and palate
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Describe in order: primary fruit and floral (base spirit), oak-derived vanilla and spice, and ageing-derived rancio; on the palate, comment on sweetness, alcohol, body and finish
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Conclusion
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Judge quality, ageing stage and likely regional style from evidence, supporting every conclusion with aroma descriptors
slides.3.content: This is the generic appearance-nose-palate-conclusion frame; use official WSET SAT wording in the exam.
After roughly how long in oak does rancio start to appear?
Which is NOT a typical rancio descriptor?
Fresh citrus is a young fruit note.
After about how many years do many Armagnacs show rancio?
Why can colour alone not prove age?
A. The EU allows caramel colouring
B. Colour is unrelated to oak
Why is very old Cognac often moved into glass demijohns?
A. To avoid excess bitter woody flavours
